nodes.desc: candor-gate — the good fence that makes good neighbors: a two-faced discipline for skills imported from another author's garden (e.g. Bryant's Gauntlet). The CANDOR face is the relational reflex worth keeping — ask first; answer a "prove it" with the proof, not a bristle; park rather than argue; name the opening as eagerly as the hazard; earn the right to say "cut that out" and be thanked for it. The GATE face is mechanical: before an imported skill acts in a shop that did not author it, it clears provenance (verify vs the author's pinned key), opt-in engagement (no silent always-on), consent for third-party or family person-facts before persistence, consent for any outward egress (local models, network), and no dangling routes. Use when installing or importing a skill, "gate this skill", "is this safe to install", "verify before I trust", or when a guard/candor call is in the air. nodes.name: containment-during-exec

nodes.desc: A design rule for bounding what EXECUTED code does WHILE it runs — the gap that before/after checks (tumblers, round-trips, attestation) leave open once you actually run transacted or client code that can change a real system. Enforcement-first options + guards: CAPABILITY-SCOPED exec (every real-world reach default-denied, each grant its own consent tumbler; the bound is the capability set, not trust in the code); an OBSERVE-ONLY boundary-view of what the run touched (honest, never deceitful); SANDBOX-REAL-vs-THEATER (only a boundary the code can't escape counts — name which you have); TWO-KEY for irreversible reaches (a live during-run consent, never a blanket pre-grant). Kept losers: "attest and check after" is proof-after in disguise; "forbid running code" is the boundary someone crosses anyway. Use it when you'll run untrusted or transacted code that can change a real system, or when "sandboxed" must be a real control, not a hope.

Its discipline is not a lock but an ACCOUNT: record consents over paths, RECTIFY when one is crossed, and speak in INCIDENT terms (forensics, not blame) if data is lost or trust could be. nodes.desc: A design rule for deciding WHICH format is the source of truth when one document lives in two forms — classically Markdown ↔ Org, but any pair (md / org / html / rst). Three stances: PER-USER (the format THIS user hand-edits is canonical, chosen by their freedom-vs-consent lean — a freedom-caring user keeps the format they edit; a consent-qualified user doesn't care, so the tool's native format wins); ORG-NATIVE (Org is authoritative, Markdown an imported/exported view); MD-NATIVE (Markdown is canonical, Org a derived rendering). The reconciliation is itself a transformer with a prove-a-promise obligation: md → org → edit → org → md must round-trip to identity, and a load-bearing change rides a durable/local semaphore (files, git-as-transport), never a wire. Use it when deciding whether Org or Markdown (or another format) should be the source of truth, when a tool wants one format but the user edits another, or when round-tripping two formats without losing structure.

nodes.name: tool-lifecycle

nodes.desc: The spell that applies a skill after the fact: take a skill (new, changed, or one that should have fired) and a prompt already answered — one C4 has registered, an advice note, or this session's own prompts — and re-run that prompt's decisions under the skill, using whatever other skills and MCP calls the re-run needs, first as flexibly as it takes and then as sparingly as reproduces the result. It produces a delta: what stands, what changes, what now goes back to the person, what was a gap. Use on "apply X retroactively", "re-run this session under the new skill", "what would X have changed", "retro-apply", "the test case is this session", "would this still come back to me", or right after a new skill lands and an old prompt is the obvious test.
